title: Text Processing with grep, sed, and awk
markdown:
# Text Processing with `grep`, `sed`, and `awk`

Linux gives you three tools that each handle a different level of text processing. `grep` finds lines that match a pattern. `sed` edits the text stream — substituting, deleting, or inserting content. `awk` treats each line as a structured record with named fields, letting you filter rows, extract columns, and compute values. Together they cover the full range of text processing tasks you'll encounter working with logs, exports, and data files.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/Text-processing.svg)

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Search and filter lines using `grep` with basic and extended patterns
- Substitute and transform text with `sed`
- Extract fields, apply row conditions, and aggregate values with `awk`

## The Scenario: Cleaning Employee Data at `Poridhi.io`

The HR team has exported employee records from three regional offices into a single file. The data arrived messy — department names have inconsistent casing, and active vs inactive employees are mixed together. Before loading into the central database, the data needs to be filtered, standardized, and summarized.

| What | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `textlab/data/employees.csv` | Raw employee export with inconsistent formatting |
| `grep` | Filter records by status, department, or pattern |
| `sed` | Standardize casing and clean field values |
| `awk` | Extract fields, count by department, compute salary averages |

## Part 1: The Three Tools at a Glance

| Tool | What it does | Best for |
|------|-------------|----------|
| `grep` | Finds lines matching a pattern | Filtering, searching |
| `sed` | Transforms text using substitution rules | Cleaning, reformatting |
| `awk` | Processes lines as structured fields | Extracting, calculating, reporting |

A common pattern is to use them in sequence: `grep` filters the relevant lines, `sed` cleans the format, and `awk` computes the result. Each one accepts piped input, so they naturally compose.

## Part 2: Setting Up the Environment

### Step 1: Create the Working Directory

```bash
mkdir -p textlab/data
```

### Step 2: Create the Employee Data File

```bash
cat > textlab/data/employees.csv << 'EOF'
id,name,department,salary,status
E001,Alice Johnson,Engineering,85000,active
E002,Bob Smith,MARKETING,72000,active
E003,Carol White,engineering,91000,inactive
E004,Dave Brown,Sales,65000,active
E005,Eve Davis,ENGINEERING,88000,active
E006,Frank Miller,Marketing,71000,active
E007,Grace Lee,sales,67000,inactive
E008,Henry Wilson,Engineering,93000,active
E009,Iris Clark,SALES,78000,active
E010,Jack Turner,marketing,69000,inactive
EOF
```

Verify the file:

```bash
cat textlab/data/employees.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/image.png)

Notice the inconsistency: `Engineering`, `ENGINEERING`, and `engineering` all refer to the same department. This is what we'll fix.

## Part 3: Searching and Filtering with `grep`

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/grep.svg)

`grep` prints every line that matches a given pattern. Basic syntax:

```
grep [options] "pattern" file
```

### Step 1: Find Lines Matching a Pattern

Find all engineering employees:

```bash
grep "Engineering" textlab/data/employees.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/image-1.png)

Only exact matches are returned — `ENGINEERING` and `engineering` are missed. Use `-i` for case-insensitive search:

```bash
grep -i "engineering" textlab/data/employees.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/image-2.png)

All three variants are returned now.

### Step 2: Filter by Status

```bash
# Active employees only (grep -w matches the whole word, not "inactive")
grep -w "active" textlab/data/employees.csv

# Inactive employees only
grep -w "inactive" textlab/data/employees.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/image-3.png)

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/image-4.png)

> **Note:** `-w` (whole word) is important here. Without it, `grep "active"` would also match "inactive" since "active" appears inside that word.

### Step 3: Invert and Count

```bash
# Count active employees
grep -cw "active" textlab/data/employees.csv

# Count inactive employees
grep -cw "inactive" textlab/data/employees.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/image-5.png)

`-c` returns a count instead of the matching lines.

**Why it matters**: `grep` is the fastest way to reduce a large file to only the relevant lines before passing them to `sed` or `awk` for further processing.

## Part 4: Transforming Text with `sed`

`sed` processes a text stream line by line, applying editing rules. The most common operation is substitution:

```
sed 's/find/replace/flags' file
```

- `g` flag — replace all occurrences per line (not just the first)
- `I` flag — case-insensitive match (GNU sed)
- `d` command — delete a line

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/sed.svg)

### Step 1: Basic Substitution

Standardize "MARKETING" to "Marketing":

```bash
sed 's/MARKETING/Marketing/g' textlab/data/employees.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/image-6.png)

This only fixes the uppercase variant. To handle all casing variants at once, use the `I` flag:

```bash
sed 's/marketing/Marketing/gI' textlab/data/employees.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/image-7.png)

### Step 2: Normalize All Department Names

Fix all three departments in one command — multiple rules are separated by `;`:

```bash
sed 's/engineering/Engineering/gI; s/marketing/Marketing/gI; s/sales/Sales/gI' \
  textlab/data/employees.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/image-8.png)

> **Note:** This doesn't save the changes to the original file — it just outputs the transformed text to the terminal. To save it, redirect the output to a new file.

### Step 3: Save the Cleaned File

```bash
sed 's/engineering/Engineering/gI; s/marketing/Marketing/gI; s/sales/Sales/gI' \
  textlab/data/employees.csv > textlab/data/employees_clean.csv
```

Verify the cleaned file:

```bash
cat textlab/data/employees_clean.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/image-9.png)

All department names are now consistently capitalized. The original file is untouched — the output went to a new file.

**Why it matters**: `sed` is ideal for bulk substitutions across large files. It processes line by line without loading the full file into memory, making it fast even on multi-gigabyte files.

## Part 5: Field Processing with `awk`

`awk` treats each line as a record split into fields by a delimiter. Use `-F` to set the field separator. Key variables:

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `$1`, `$2`, `$3`... | Fields by position |
| `NR` | Current line (record) number |
| `NF` | Number of fields on the current line |

### Step 1: Extract Specific Columns

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/awk.svg)

In our CSV, the fields are: `id` (1), `name` (2), `department` (3), `salary` (4), `status` (5). Print only the name and department columns from the cleaned file:

```bash
awk -F',' 'NR > 1 {print $2, $3}' textlab/data/employees_clean.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/image-10.png)

`NR > 1` skips the header row. `-F','` sets the comma as the field separator. `print $2, $3` outputs the name and department fields.

### Step 2: Filter Rows by Field Value

Print only Engineering employees with their salary:

```bash
awk -F',' '$3 == "Engineering" {print $2, $4}' textlab/data/employees_clean.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/image-11.png)

Print active employees earning more than 80,000:

```bash
awk -F',' 'NR > 1 && $5 == "active" && $4 > 80000 {print $2, $3, $4}' textlab/data/employees_clean.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/image-12.png)

### Step 3: Aggregate — Count and Average

Count employees per department:

```bash
awk -F',' 'NR > 1 {count[$3]++} END {for (dept in count) print count[dept], dept}' \
  textlab/data/employees_clean.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/image-13.png)

Here, `count[$3]++` increments the counter for the department in field 3. The `END` block runs after all lines are processed and prints the count for each department. The for loop iterates over the unique department names in the `count` array.

Calculate the average salary of active employees:

```bash
awk -F',' 'NR > 1 && $5 == "active" {sum += $4; n++} END {printf "Average salary: $%.0f\n", sum/n}' \
  textlab/data/employees_clean.csv
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2011/images/image-14.png)

The `END` block runs once, after all lines are processed — perfect for totals and averages.

**Why it matters**: `awk` turns flat text files into structured data. It can filter by value, group by field, and do arithmetic — without a database or scripting language.

## Conclusion

In this lab, we used all three tools on the same dataset — each adding a layer the others couldn't handle alone:

- `grep` filtered records by pattern and status
- `sed` cleaned and standardized the inconsistent department names
- `awk` extracted columns, applied numeric filters, and computed summary statistics

The standard production pattern: pipe `grep` output into `sed` to clean it, then into `awk` to report on it. All three accept piped input, so they compose naturally into a single command line.
